units.text: From Modelling to Assessing Algorithmic Abstraction -the Missing Dimension
INTRODUCTION

Solving algorithmic problems is a core practice of computer science (CS).Computer scientists solve algorithmic problems from different fields, using a variety of mental tools.Some are general problem-solving tools, also used for example, for solving mathematical problems or design problems.These tools include strategies such as divide-and-conquer, heuristics such as analogies or generalizations of specific cases, and control methods, such as reflection.However, algorithmic problem solving also has some distinct characteristics.

One such characteristic is abstraction, which is widely acknowledged as a powerful and central idea in CS, which is used in multiple forms in every aspect of CS [4].In algorithmic problem solving, abstraction is first used to reformulate the given problem, simplifying it by modelling the problem world and omitting non-relevant details while maintaining the essence of the problem.For example, the classic reformulation of navigation problems employs graphs to model the problem world and abstracts a navigation problem by an equivalent graph problem, such as finding a shortest path.Abstraction is also used for gradually devising the solution at different levels of specificity until an unambiguous and sufficiently specific algorithm is obtained.The solution can then be translated into a program written in a specific programming language.

Being a core practice of CS, algorithmic problem solving is at the center of most introductory CS courses, at all grade levels.In many of them, especially those intended for a younger audience, the solution process involves the translation phase, namely, programming, as well as the experimental phase of executing the programmed artifacts.Moreover, often introductory courses focus only (or almost only) on the programming aspect.The students are introduced to a specific programming language or programming environment, and devise programs that solve given problems.However, such courses may in fact be programming courses rather than CS courses, since they do not emphasize the key aspects of problem solving that precede the programming phase and that make the most of abstraction.Although programming courses have their merit, they cannot be considered as CS courses, since CS is more than just programming [15].CS introductory courses should expose students to the entire core process of algorithmic problem solving, starting with the phases of reformulating and obtaining insight into a given problem and devising an algorithm to solve it, and then implementing this algorithm in a programming language and examining the solution by executing the program.This holistic approach inherently involves the idea of abstraction, specifically the type of abstraction used during the algorithmic problem-solving process -algorithmic abstraction.Following Bruner [12] and his spiral curriculum framework, this approach is highly suitable for introductory courses, including those intended for very young learners, since an early (age-appropriate) treatment of abstraction supports and fosters its meaningful learning.In addition, students are exposed to a more coherent and honest representation of the nature of the discipline (as opposed to one limited only to programming).Since abstraction is a core component of computational thinking (CT) [49,50], such a holistic introduction to CS may also promote the development of CT.

The holistic approach necessitates effective methods to teach algorithmic abstraction as well as effective assessment frameworks.Several such methods and frameworks are available in the literature and some of them will be presented in Section 2. In this paper, we present a generalized model for assessing algorithmic abstraction in different educational contexts.This model has the advantage of being rooted in both known and frequently used theoretical models and empirical research results; thus, it combines top-down (deductive) and bottom-up (inductive) perspectives [8].It builds on the results of two studies conducted in our research group (denoted hereafter as Study 1 and Study 2, respectively), which examined the manifestation and use of algorithmic abstraction in different educational contexts.Both studies employed a similar model of assessment, but each found grounded evidence that extended this model differently.By examining and gaining insights into these extensions and their meaning, we were able to form a generalized perspective that could accommodate both extensions.Employing this perspective, we defined a new dimension and integrated it into the original model by using a Cartesian product.The resulting model included all the components of the original model, the two extensions that were found in the two studies, as well as new components that were introduced by the Cartesian product.All the new components have not emerged in either Study 1 or Study 2; however, each can be matched as an appropriate code for a basic unit that can be found in some educational event that concerns algorithmic problem solving (e.g., a content unit in a written solution from a student or a discourse unit in an episode of problem solving taking place in a CS class).

Hence, in the spirit of grounded theory, we obtained a generalized and more expressive model, which offers deeper insights into the concept of algorithmic abstraction and can be used for more insightful future evaluations and explorations of the teaching and learning of algorithmic abstraction.

This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents relevant background and related research results.Section 3 describes Study 1 [31] and Study 2 [19], thus providing the context required for building on part of their results to obtain the new generalized model, which will be presented in Section 4. We discuss the new model in Section 5.
BACKGROUND AND LITERATURE REVIEW

This section presents relevant background and research literature.Section 2.1 discusses the fundamental CS idea of abstraction.Section 2.2 expands on the role that abstraction plays in algorithmic problem solving.Section 2.3 focuses on teaching and learning algorithmic abstraction, and Section 2.4 deals with assessing it.
Abstraction

In general, abstraction is a powerful cognitive tool, which can be employed in almost every context and form of thinking and doing.Theories of children's cognitive development strongly emphasize the role of abstraction and use abstraction-related terms for describing different cognitive levels [10,12,34,[36][37][38]43]. Abstraction is especially, although not solely, related to advanced developmental cognitive phases [39].Some theories also consider abstraction as a necessary tool for achieving advancements in cognitive development [10,30] or throughout conceptual learning processes, where learners advance throughout sequences of perception levels with increasing conceptual depth [10,12].

As a general idea, which crosses disciplines and areas, the essence of abstraction is about ignoring details in order to achieve a certain level of simplification that allows one to focus on core aspects, as is done by an artist who creates abstract paintings, a mathematician who defines new concepts in topology, a scientist who models a natural phenomenon, or a cartographer who draws a map of a city.Abstraction abilities are required both by the creators and the users of abstract artifacts, such as visitors who are expected to find their way around a city despite the missing details in the map.

In CS, abstraction is used in different CS contexts and is manifested in different ways.For example, it is used in computational models such as automata and for abstract data types.The focus on core aspects, whether by neglecting details or by getting along despite missing details serves two prevalent CS purposes.First, it enables a change in resolution, allowing one to see the "big picture" instead of just a collection of metaphoric pixels that compose it, i.e., the forest rather than the trees.Ignoring the right amount of details by identifying the appropriate resolution (where appropriateness depends on context) may optimize the cognitive load required for performing CS activities of various sorts or it may optimize the quality of outcomes.For example, programming in assembly languages requires one to pay attention to very small details, an effort that is spared when programming in a high-level language.Nevertheless, working at the machine level may be necessary in certain contexts.Second, the focus on core aspects fosters generalizations.For example, in object-oriented design the focus on joint properties allows one to consider different items as manifestations of the same entity.Note that abstraction is present even in those aspects of CS that are considered concrete.For example, when learning a programming language, a template of a programming statement such as if <Boolean condition> {then {<if-block>} else {<else-block}>} is an abstraction that generalizes an infinite set of concrete programming statements.Moreover, even in environments intended for young children, abstraction cannot be avoided.For example, the Scratch block constitutes an abstraction of an infinite set of instructions, where each one is obtained by including a value in the empty part of the block.

The immense importance of abstraction in CS was explicitly highlighted by CS experts whenever the (still debatable) nature of the discipline was addressed.Wing referred to abstraction as "the essence of computational thinking" [50, p. 3717], namely, what computer scientists constantly do -create abstractions and use them when practicing and researching CS.For Wing, the created abstractions are "the mental tools of computing" [50, p. 3718].For Aho and Ullman, CS is "the science of abstraction" [2, p. 1], whereas Dijkstra, 20 years before, highlighted the "effective exploitation of" one's "powers of abstraction" as the most vital activity a CS expert is engaged with" [16, p. 864].For Dijkstra, the importance of abstraction was expressed by it being "the only mental tool by means of which a very finite piece of reasoning can cover a myriad of cases" [16, p. 864].Namely, Dijkstra valued the generalization powers of abstraction.In contrast, Knuth and Hartmanis emphasized the changes in resolution: "simultaneously seeing things "in the large" and "in the small"" (Knuth, in [24], p.39), and "One of the defining characteristics of computer science is the immense difference in scale of the phenomena CS deals with.From the individual bits of program and data in the computers to billions of operations per second on this information by the highly complex machines, their operating systems, and the various languages in which the problems are described, the scale changes through many orders of magnitude" (Hartmanis, in [24], p. 39).Apparently, Knuth considered any kind of resolution, whereas Hartmanis focused on magnitude from a physical-technological point of view.Other, more abstract resolutions are also used in CS, such as the resolution of meaning, which will be discussed in Section 2.3.

Hartmanis' words illuminate an important difference between the nature of CS abstraction and the abstraction encapsulated in a simple printed map: in CS, abstractions are often performed repeatedly over a scale of abstraction-concreteness.Each act of abstraction takes us further up the scale, zooming out along the scale of resolution towards the 'big picture', farther away from its individual (metaphoric) pixels, and even farther away from the (metaphoric) bits that compose the pixels.When abstractions are reversed, increasingly smaller details are gradually revealed, yielding more concrete representations as one zooms in down the scale.Others, such as Knuth [24] and Wing [49], preferred the image of hierarchies of levels over the image of scales.In such hierarchies, each act of abstraction takes us one level up, and computer scientists employ their ability to "rapidly change levels of abstraction" [24, p. 39], or even think at multiple levels at the same time [49].
Abstraction in algorithmic problem solving

As noted in the introduction, abstraction is inherent in algorithmic problem solving.Barnes,Fincher,and Thompson [9] adapted Polya's model for mathematical problem solving, "how to solve it?"[40] to CS, resulting in the model "how to program it?".Their model consists of four stages: understanding, design, writing, and review.In the first stage, solvers need to fully understand the description of the problem and ask themselves 'what if' questions (e.g., when trying to find the maximum between two numbers, ask yourselfwhat if both numbers are equal?).In addition, they should think of representing input-output examples, to help them understand both typical and extreme specific cases.In the second stage, solvers need to look for similar problems that they have already solved and use their experience while trying to decide which strategy to use.This stage is about planning and designing an algorithm, namely, a description of a solution, formulated by a finite set of unambiguous components, which can be entirely independent of any programming language.Solvers can use any graphical means or pseudo-code in order to remain at the algorithmic design level and avoid dealing with implementation details at this stage (thus fostering abstraction).In the third stage, solvers need to transform their design into a written program in a specific programming language.The last stage involves reviewing the solution, for example, by executing the written program, and reflecting as well as learning lessons from the final solution and the process of problem solving.This stage is important for building up the solver's experience for use in future problem-solving situations.We will now elaborate on these stages, focusing on the role of abstraction.

The process starts by examining the problem at hand and gaining insights into it.As experts of algorithmic problems [5], computer scientists are often faced with contextualized problems, defined and described in terms of different knowledge areas.For example, problems that concern genetics and genetic mapping or problems that concern grammatical analysis of a text written in a natural language.The former may be described in terms of DNA and other genetics-related professional terms and the latter may use grammatical terms such as sentences, objects, subjects, nouns, and adjectives.The first step is modelling the problem, abstracting away professional terms specific to the knowledge area to which the problem belongs and representing it with neutral terms.Genetics-related problems can be described by means of matching patterns in strings of characters, whereas problems dealing with grammatical analysis can be described in terms of hierarchic sequences of composite and atomic abstract objects.Then, the solver should think about the abstract problem and its characteristics.At this time, the solver may recognize similar problems that may motivate the use of analogies or reduction [6].For example, a certain similarity between a problem in genetics and a problem that deals with text editors may be revealed only after both are modeled by means of strings of characters.As stressed by Ginat [20], gaining deep enough insights into the problem often leads to more elegant and even more efficient solutions [22].In this phase, one may also decide which problem-solving paradigm is most appropriate.

After the solver understands the algorithmic problem at hand and gains insights into it, it is time to start devising a solution, an algorithm.Abstraction is reflected in this phase in two ways: First, an algorithm is an abstract solution.Unlike a program, which is described in terms of a specific programming language, an algorithm is general and independent of any language.Hence, although it includes only unambiguous steps, they can be described in a high-level natural language, which necessarily ignores details.For example, one may write 'sum the two numbers' and then 'print the sum', without thinking about how the numbers are summed or printed.Second, as a manifestation of using levels of abstraction, the solution may be constructed gradually, starting from general algorithms, and then developing them into more concrete ones by adding more details, until reaching an algorithm that is sufficiently detailed (yet abstract, since it ignores programming details).For example, a relatively abstract solution may include the step 'search for Mary in the list of students', whereas a more concrete algorithm will replace this step with an algorithmic description of performing a search in a sorted list.The level of concreteness that should be reached is context dependent.These levels use a resolution of meaning, alternating between 'what' and 'how'.For example, the step 'search for Mary in the list of students' describes what should be done, a search for the desired item.The more detailed solution describes how this search is done.Note that the relation "whathow" also holds between the problem (what is to be done) and the obtained algorithm (how it should be done).As viewed by Dijkstra, "[T]his oscillation between "the representation" and "what it stands for" is an intrinsic part of the programmer's game" [17 p. 1].Thus, Dijkstra considers a lower-level solution as a concrete representation of a higher-level one.By generalization, one may view the resulting algorithm as a more concrete representation of the problem at hand.

Once a sufficiently specified algorithm is reached, one can translate it to a concrete representation of it, i.e., a program that implements the solution in a specific programming language.Although being rather concrete, a program still maintains some level of abstraction since it is general and is intended to handle all possible inputs.This generalization disappears, however, when the program is run on a specific machine with a specific input.

Note that in general, the process may be iterative, also involving going up from a certain level to a more abstract one.Thus, using Dijkstra's terms, it describes a cognitive oscillating process that is more general than top-down development.The use of abstraction throughout this process, as detailed above, is algorithmic abstraction.

Dale and Walker [14] distinguished between two types of abstraction in CS problem solving: procedural abstraction and data abstraction.Procedural abstraction inherently involves the alternation between 'what' and 'how', as mentioned above.Data abstraction is used for abstracting the details of representing data of different sorts by means of abstract data types (ADTs).In the context of algorithmic problem solving, data abstraction may be employed when modeling a contextualized problem, representing it in CS terms.Data abstraction may also be used when the need for a certain ADT arises during the algorithmic solution process.Revealing or hiding details that concern data structures are also manifestations of alternating between levels of abstraction that correspond to meaning -the more abstract level of what kind of data is stored in the ADT and what kinds of operations can be performed on the ADT, and the more concrete level of how the ADT and its operations are implemented.
Learning and teaching algorithmic abstraction

Many studies, dealing with different CS contexts and different age levels, have indicated that students' understanding and use of abstraction are insufficient, thus pointing to an educational challenge (e.g., in the context of object-oriented programming, data structures, and the use of reduction [1, 6, 33, respectively]).This was also shown regarding algorithmic abstraction [e.g., 23].Different approaches have been suggested for teaching abstraction, either implicit [e.g., 27], where abstraction is extensively used in appropriate courses, or explicit ones [26], where explicit emphasis is put on abstraction.The latter is consistent with Bruner's approach [12] as well as with different frameworks for meaningful learning [e.g., 7], according to which an explicit approach is more effective for achieving meaningful learning and particularly regarding complex and multi-facet ideas, such as abstraction.

According to Armoni [4,, in the context of algorithmic problem solving, having good algorithmic abstraction ability means, among other things, being able to 1) differentiate between levels of abstraction; 2) move freely and consciously between levels of abstraction; 3) decide, in every phase of the problem-solving process, at which level of abstraction it is appropriate to work; and 4) use successive refinements of abstraction.

Perennet, Groote, and Kaasenbrod [35] used the perspective of representations and defined a hierarchy (hereafter referred to as the PGK hierarchy) that describes a collection of representations of the algorithm concept, whereas a higher level is an abstract representation of a lower one, and a lower level is a concrete representation of a higher one.In particular, this hierarchy expresses the relation mentioned above, whereby an algorithm is a concrete representation of a problem:

• Level 4, the Problem level: The highest level of the hierarchy represents an algorithm by the problem it solves (what), a black box that hides the implementation details (how).• Level 3, the Object level: This level refers to an algorithm as an object that solves a problem and is independent of a specific programming language.• Level 2, the Program level: At this level, an algorithm is an executable program in a specific programming language.• Level 1, the Execution level: The lowest level of the hierarchy, which refers to a specific run of a program, on a specific input and a specific machine.

This hierarchy was inspired by Hazzan's framework [25], according to which learners unconsciously tend to perceive a newly introduced concept at a level of abstraction that is lower than the appropriate one.Using a cognitive perspective, Perrenet et al. defined their hierarchy for modeling the abstraction levels in which one can perceive the concept of an algorithm, and used it to assess undergraduate students' perceptions of this concept [35].

Armoni [4] observed that in addition to consisting of representations of the concept of an algorithm, the PGK hierarchy can also be viewed as a representation of the phases of the algorithmic problem-solving process, namely, the four levels of Problem, Algorithm, Program, and Execution correspond to the phases of Barnes et al. 's model -understanding, design, writing, and review.We find the names of the PGK levels better for describing these phases, since they reflect their CS meaning.Armoni posited that the PGK hierarchy can be used to guide a teaching process that aims at teaching algorithmic abstraction, and specifically for acquiring the four abilities listed above.From this point of view, a more appropriate name for the object level (Level 3) is the Algorithm level [4], since in the context of algorithmic problem solving, this level captures what is commonly and popularly referred to as an "algorithm" -a solution that is not presented in a specific programming language but instead is composed of unambiguous instructions in a natural language.Consequently, she suggested a framework for explicit teaching of algorithmic abstraction [4], using the PGK hierarchy (in which Level 3 is renamed as the Algorithm level) as a central teaching aid.

Among the teaching guidelines included in this framework are the following [4]: (1) Be persistent and precise -the teacher must be clear about the current level of abstraction in use and take care not to discuss several levels at the same time.(2) Use linguistic aids to distinguish between levels of abstraction, for example, programming language-related terms should be used only below Level 3. (3) Order from high to low -discussions should start at a high level of abstraction and go down only when a concrete treatment is required.( 4) Use refinements of Level 3 -due to the students' tendency to ignore this level and not recognize its importance, it should not be skipped over, and moreover (in line with the third guideline above), it should even be extended by a top-down process of algorithm design in which an algorithm is fully developed before moving to Level 2. (5) Be explicit, also using reflection.As clarified by Statter and Armoni [45], and in line with the process of problem solving as described in Section 2.2, the third guideline means that discussions should start from higher levels of the hierarchy (starting with Level 4 of the problem) and then oscillate between the levels as appropriate, going down to lower levels only when a more concrete treatment is required.The highlighted fragment, which uses Dijkstra's term of oscillation ( [17], see Section 2.2) stresses that one should not cling to a lower level upon arriving to it, but instead, go up again to a higher level when appropriate.For example, after a bug was detected in Levels 1 and 2, one may recognize the need to amend the solution and go up to the Algorithm level to identify and perform appropriate corrections, instead of making the corrections at the Program level.Statter and Armoni [45] showed that an implementation of Armoni's framework in an introductory CS course for 7 th -graders was very effective and that after only a short preparation, the teachers successfully applied it, except for tending to neglect the second principle of linguistic aids.

Waite et al. [47] also turned to the PGK hierarchy as a guide for teaching programming in elementary schools (K-5).To fit the young age of the students and the weaker CS background of the teachers, they decided to make the levels more concrete, renaming them as Problem, Design, Code, and Running the Code, respectively.Following a preliminary qualitative study with five teachers [47], which examined the abstraction levels and the related vocabulary used by the teachers during reflective interviews, they decided to rename the higher level as "Task".They used the acronym LOA (Levels of Abstraction) to denote this model.Their Design level could be interpreted as a planning phase, and thus represent a limited view of an algorithm, namely, an initial phase of the solution rather than a solution in itself.On the one hand, as Waite et al. conjectured, a more concrete approach may be necessary for K-5 teachers and their learners.On the other hand, however, the highly concrete representation may affect teachers' and learners' perceptions of algorithmic abstraction.More research is required to determine whether teachers and learners who follow Waite et al. 's version of the PGK hierarchy succeed in internalizing this concept.Since algorithmic abstraction is a core concept of CS, failing to develop an (age-appropriate) reliable perception of it might lead to a faulty image of CS and undesired misconceptions of its nature.Waite et al. 's LOA model has impacted the current K-12 computing curriculum in England [32], specifically the two major strands of programming and algorithms, which emphasize the model and its meaning.

Liebe and Camp [28] also used reflective interviews to investigate the teaching of abstraction in CS by K-12 CS teachers of different age levels.The teachers' answers were based on their own views of abstraction, which were often limited.The findings indicated that the teachers lacked professional training regarding abstraction, were unsure what abstraction abilities the students needed to acquire, and tended not to assess abstraction.Only a few of them referred to levels of abstraction.

Rahimi, Barendsen, and Henze [41] presented an instructional model to guide the enhancement of algorithmic thinking of highschool students by a fusion of designing and conceptual learning.This involved creating intermediate design products a cycle of four phases, somewhat corresponding to the levels of the PGK hierarchy.Reflective interviews with four teachers and group interviews with their students indicated that this instructional model facilitated skills related to algorithmic abstraction.Ginat [21] studied a didactic intervention in an undergraduate course on algorithm problem solving, for which the students were required to have some CS knowledge (including CS1 And CS2).The intervention emphasized the first phase of gaining insight into the problem at hand, consistently and explicitly using declarative observations (i.e., at the Problem level) rather than operational ones (i.e., at the Algorithm or Program levels), where the former observations led to better solutions (in terms of correctness, elegance, or efficiency).His findings indicated that the intervention was effective in improving students' abstraction ability, as manifested in their improved ability to perform declarative observations and reach better solutions.
Assessing algorithmic abstraction
Assessing algorithmic abstraction is relevant for both teachers and students, to evaluate how teachers perceive and teach algorithmic abstraction and how students perceive and perform it.

Cutts et al. [13] developed "the abstraction transition taxonomy", to assess the extent to which abstraction is reflected in tasks that teachers pose to their students (during the teaching process or summative assessments).It consists of three levels of abstraction: English, CS speak, and Code.Cutts et al. used it to examine the transitions between abstraction levels that the students had to make when performing certain tasks, specifically the transitions between the starting and end point of a given task.For example, a multiplechoice question that requires the students to identify the problem solved by a given code segment was considered as a transition from the Code level to the English level.They did not consider the levels of abstraction that may have been used throughout the problem-solving process (in-between the starting and end points, respectively) [45].

Ginat and Blau [22] evaluated the abstraction ability of preservice teachers.Their interpretation of abstraction referred to the sophistication of the solutions, in terms of the conceptual gap between the solution and the problem it was designed to solve.Straightforward solutions were induced directly from the problem's description, whereas more sophisticated solvers strived to rise above the specific description and identify alternative presentations.Their tool included three diagnostic algorithmic problems; each had several solutions, differing on the degree of abstraction they employed, in terms of sophistication.These differences were rooted in the depth of the insight gained during the first phase of the problem-solving solution.Their perspective is very relevant in teaching and assessing abstraction in problem solving [e.g., 3,6], but it does not capture the entire scope of algorithmic abstraction.

Quite a few tools or methods have been developed to assess K-12 students' CT skills, including abstraction.Some of them use diagnostic tasks [e.g., 48], whereas others are generic and can be used with any problem that the students may encounter [e.g., 44].Some examine students' problem-solving process [e.g., 11], whereas other only examine the resulting artifacts [e.g., 44].However, most do not attempt to evaluate the full-range process of algorithmic abstraction and often deal only with the lower level of programming.Moreover, as noted by Armoni [5], the interpretation of abstraction in the context of CT tends to be narrow and far from reflecting the full essence of algorithmic abstraction.For example, in Brennan and Resnick's framework of CT [11], abstraction was only mentioned as part of the practice, "abstracting and modularizing", although each of the other three practices included in their framework inherently necessitates a manifestation of abstraction (e.g., reusing and remixing).Similarly, in CT, Román-Gonzáles et al.'s widely used CT test [42], abstraction is assessed only by students' use of functions.

Statter and Armoni [45] measured algorithmic abstraction among 7th-graders in the context of a block-based programming environment.Their assessment was based on the PGK hierarchy as representing the process of algorithmic problem solving [35], Armoni's approach [4] for teaching algorithmic abstraction, and her formulation of good algorithmic abstraction ability [4], as mentioned in Section 2.3.Consequently, they defined an operational definition for algorithmic abstraction consisting of six indicators that directly indicate the use of algorithmic abstraction, all of which relate to the PGK hierarchy: using an algorithm (Level 3), working only at the Algorithm level, when appropriate (Level 3), using black boxes (Level 4), being able to distinguish between the four levels of algorithmic abstraction (Levels 1-4), being able to move freely between the four levels of algorithmic abstraction (Levels 1-4), and being able to decide at which of the four levels of algorithmic abstraction to work (Levels 1-4).In addition, they used four indicators that can be used as corroborative evidence of algorithmic abstraction ability (e.g., providing explanations for solutions and the perception of the nature of CS).They used diagnostic tasks (in exams and interviews); however, their approach can be used to assess algorithmic abstraction during the solution process of any algorithmic problem.

Faber et al. [18] also turned to the PGK hierarchy to design a tool for assessing the abstraction abilities of 5-6-year-old children, when solving algorithmic tasks by programming an educational robot.They used Waite et al. 's variant of the PGK hierarchy [46], in which the Algorithm and Programming levels were renamed as the Design and Code levels, respectively.They analyzed students' work when solving tasks and constructed a rubric in which observed behaviors were assigned to levels of abstraction.In their data set, whenever engaging with design, the students referred to the specific robot, its properties and programming language, although this level is supposed to be independent of any implementation.This caused the researchers to split the Design level into two levels: the Abstract Design level and the Concrete Design level.However, they reasoned that since the robot was known a-priori as the tool with which the tasks are to be solved, it did not make sense to design without referring to the robot's programming language; hence, the Design Level is necessarily concrete.Namely, they assumed that in the context of robotics, students can work at a higher level of abstraction, without using implementation-related terms, only when they are unaware of a concrete implementation, and they cannot ignore the details of such an implementation once it is known.In other words, in their assessment tool, the Design level, which is supposed to be abstract, had collapsed into a concrete one that uses programming-related terms.
THE CONTEXT

In the last few years, two doctoral research projects, Study 1 and Study 2, have been conducted in our research group by the first and second authors, respectively, under the supervision of the third author.They constituted the ground from which our generalized assessment model has emerged.In this section we describe the two studies and the assessment models they used.As described below, both studies started with a model based on the PGK hierarchy, and in both studies the data led to modifying the basic model, by adding a new level of abstraction.
Study 1: Algorithmic abstraction in an introductory high-school CS course

The first research project [31] focused on teaching the fundamentals of CS in high school and studied the effect of certain aspects of teachers' practice on their students' algorithmic abstraction ability.Specifically, it examined the teachers' underlying instructional approaches and the ways they employed algorithmic abstraction in their teaching practice.Their use of algorithmic abstraction in their teaching was assessed by analyzing problem-solving episodes initiated by the teachers in class.This was a qualitative content analysis of the transcripts obtained through recorded class observations.It started in a deductive content analysis [8], based on the PGK hierarchy.The teachers' discourse was analyzed, using the four levels of the PGK hierarchy as a 4-category system, by identifying the levels of abstraction used by the teachers during the analyzed episodes.An initial phase was performed to examine the appropriateness of the 4-category system for the analyzed data, specifically to find out whether additional categories emerged from the data, besides the basic four ones.This initial analysis yielded a finding from which a new category emerged.In a typical problem-solving episode, after introducing an algorithmic problem in class, the teachers conducted algorithmic discussions during which a solution for the given problem was devised.However, in the data we could distinguish between higher-level discourse units and lower-level ones, used in such discussions.For example, from the perspective of abstraction, the discourse unit "first, what will be the condition of the loop?", accompanied by writing on the whiteboard an empty loop header that is very similar to the Java loop header, is very different from the unit "when should we stop reading numbers?"accompanied by writing natural-language wording to represent the header of an algorithmic conditional iterative control structure.Similarly, the discourse unit "in every execution of the loop, we will add the new value to the variable 'sum"', accompanied by Java-like writing on the whiteboard, is very different from the unit "whenever we read a new number, we should add it to our accumulator" accompanied by writing a corresponding natural-language description.The second units in both examples used clear algorithmic natural-language vocabulary, whereas the first ones used programming-related terms, Java-like English wording for steps in the algorithm (and sometimes even integrated short fragments of programming code).We saw the need to use different categories for differentiating between such discourse units.The category "Algorithm level" was not appropriate for the lower-level ones, since the Algorithm level refers to a solution that is independent of a specific programming language.The category "Program level" was not appropriate either, since the solution was not written as a program; it was a high-level description that ignored certain details.

To address the need for differentiation, the 4-category system was refined and the category "Algorithm level" was split into two sub-categories: the "Pure Algorithm level" and the "Program-Algorithm level", reflecting segments of data in which algorithmic discussions were held at the Program level (Level 2).This echoes the study by Faber et al. [18] mentioned in Section 2.4., who first conjectured that the Design level should be split into two levels, which they named as the Abstract Design Layer and the Concrete Design layer, where the latter involved terms from the robot's programming language.However, as described in Section 2.4, they omitted the first level, arguing that when the implementation tool is known a-priory, it does not make sense to create a design without referring to the specific tool and its implementation language.The data of Study 1 show that creating an algorithmic design while ignoring the details of a certain programming language, in line with the PGK hierarchy, is possible.Moreover, it is even recommended, in line with Armoni's framework [4].Thus, the two sub-categories for Level 3 are necessary.
Study 2: The assessment of a primary-school CS curriculum

The second research project examined the evolution of a new CS curriculum for 4th-grade, from the vision of the policymakers to the attained curriculum.It started by identifying the educational goals set by different policymakers and continued by analyzing the operationalization of these goals in the 4 th -grade elaborate formal curriculum.Since one of the goals set by the policymakers was to develop abstraction abilities, the different representations of the 4 th -grade curriculum, starting with the formal one, were analyzed (among other analyses) from the perspective of abstraction.To this end, the 90-page 4th-grade formal curriculum was analyzed, and like Study 1, the PGK hierarchy was used as a 4-category system in a deductive document analysis [8], starting with an initial phase in which the completeness of this system was examined.

In this case too, the initial analysis phase yielded a finding from which a new category emerged.The problems included in the formal curriculum (intended to serve as worked examples or assignments) were of two types: The first type involved problems that were described using general terms, independent of programming-related details.Such problems can be understood by CS laymen, even if they do not know how to solve them.According to Armoni [4], when teaching abstraction in CS, it is best to use such problems, since they better demonstrate the first phase of the algorithmic problem-solving process (corresponding to the Problem level of the PGK hierarchy), in which problems are modeled and the focus is on gaining insight into the problems at hand, before thinking about how they can be solved.Moreover, such problems demonstrate better the nature of CS, as a discipline that deals with different kinds of problems from different areas, and the authentic process of problem solving.The second type of problems included problems that explicitly referred to Scratch (the programming language used in this curriculum).For example: "Write a script in which upon receiving the message 'Hi' from the dog, the cat says, 'Good morning'".In contrast, a similar problem but at a higher level of abstraction is: "Create an animation in which the dog and the cat are in the yard.When the dog says 'Hi', the cat says, 'Good morning'".Although the first example is an algorithmic problem, it cannot be considered as a manifestation of the highest level of the PGK hierarchy.Terms such as 'script' or terms related to the Scratch message-passing mechanism are too close to the Program level; hence, the first example does not emphasize the gap between the levels in terms of abstraction.It also might encourage the students to move straight from the problem to programming, skipping the Algorithm level.We saw the need to distinguish between these two types of problems, and hence, added a new category between the Problem level and the Algorithm level, named the Program-Problem level.
A GENERALIZED ASSESSMENT MODEL

In this section we describe our generalized model for assessing algorithmic abstraction in algorithmic problem solving.Section 4.1 reflects on those findings of Studies 1 and 2 that were mentioned in Section 3 and extends them to a generalized assessment model.Sections 4.2-4.4explain the three parts of the generalized model, respectively.
Extending the perspective

The categories that emerged from the data of Study 1 and the data of Study 2 (Sections 3.1 and 3.2, respectively) share a common characteristic: They both capture situations in which a certain phase in the algorithmic problem-solving process is conducted at an abstraction level that is lower than the appropriate one.In Study 2, the situation was a problem phase that involved terms that belong in Level 2, instead of staying at Level 4, Similarly, in Study 1, the situation was an algorithmic problem-solving phase that involved terms that belong in Level 2, instead of staying at Level 3.

In Section 2.3, we mentioned Armoni's observation [4] that the PGK hierarchy can be viewed as a representation of the phases of the algorithmic problem-solving process, making it is useful for guiding the teaching of algorithmic problem solving.However, apparently in this context, when the emphasis is on a problem-solving process that is performed at the appropriate levels of abstraction, a more accurate way of putting this is as follows: The PGK hierarchy can be viewed as a representation of the phases of the algorithmic problem-solving process along with their appropriate level of abstraction.Thus, each level of the PGK hierarchy depicts a phase of the problem-solving process, as well as a level of abstraction.Using a mathematical formulation, when modeling a good algorithmic problem-solving process, one that demonstrates Armoni's characteristics for good algorithmic abstraction ability ( [4], see Section 2.3), each level of the PGK hierarchy represents an ordered pair (i, i), where 1 ≤ i ≤ 4, the first element represents a phase in the problem-solving process, and the second element represents a level of abstraction that is appropriate for that phase.

Obviously, since for each level the same number is used for both elements, the pair notation is redundant, and a single number is sufficient.However, as demonstrated in Section 3, when aiming to employ the PGK hierarchy as an assessment model, rather than a teaching guide, the pair notation is useful.Using this notation, the new category in the assessment model that emerged from the data of Study 1, the Program-Algorithm level, can be represented as (3, 2), whereas the new category that emerged from the data of Study 2, the Program-Problem level, can be represented as (4, 2).In both cases, the first element, which represents a phase in the problem-solving process, is greater than the second element, which represents a level of abstraction, thus reflecting the common characteristics described in the beginning of this section.

A 2-dimensional extension of the PGK hierarchy naturally follows.The first dimension uses the PGK terms, Problem, Algorithm, Program, and Execution, but corresponds to the phases of algorithmic problem solving.The second dimension corresponds to levels of abstraction, using the same identifiers.This is a Cartesian square of the PGK hierarchy, and we will denote it by PAPE 2 .Figure 1 depicts a graphical representation of this model.
In Figure 1, three primary parts can be identified, corresponding to three different situations, respectively:

• The diagonal (green) depicts an appropriate algorithmic problem-solving process, in which every phase is performed at an appropriate level of abstraction.• The lower part (red) represents working at abstraction levels that are lower than the appropriate ones.• The upper part (orange) represents working at abstraction levels that are higher than the appropriate ones.

We argue that PAPE 2 can serve as a basis for an assessment model for algorithmic abstraction.Obviously, it is at least as expressive as the PGK-based model, because every data set that can be analyzed using the PGK-based model can be analyzed using PAPE 2 , by replacing for each data unit the code i with the code (i, i).We already know that it is more expressive than the PGK-based model, since we showed two data sets from different educational contexts (a formal curriculum and teaching episodes), for which the PGK-based model was insufficient, but PAPE 2 is, capturing two different situations using one set of codes with consistent notations.In fact, as will be demonstrated in Sections 4.3 and 4.4 below, there are many more situations from problem-solving-related contexts, which can be expressed using PAPE 2 .Moreover, for each code of PAPE 2 there exists a situation that is expressed by this code.In the following sections (4.2-4.4),we elaborate on each of the three parts of PAPE 2 , respectively.
The diagonal -using appropriate levels of algorithmic abstraction

As noted above, the diagonal is a pair-representation of the PGK hierarchy, where each level represents a pair of a phase of the algorithm problem-solving process and its appropriate level of abstraction.Interestingly, this perspective is in a sense consistent with the linguistic aid, presented by Armoni [4] as one of the principles of her framework for teaching abstraction.According to this principle, in each phase of the problem-solving solution, instructors should pay attention to using an appropriate terminology, thus making the distinction between the phases even more explicit.For example, the vocabulary of a programming language ("reserved words") belongs in the programming phase, whereas in the algorithm phase it is better to avoid this vocabulary and instead use natural language words.For instance, when employing the algorithmic control structure of iteration, one can use the wording as long as instead of the word while.Furthermore, at the algorithm phase, synonyms of natural words can be used interchangeably, or as deemed appropriate by their context.Similarly, algorithm names, such as Bubble Sort or BFS belong in the algorithm phase, whereas in the problem phase one should only use general terms that refer to the problem at hand, e.g., sort, or find the shortest path [45].The explicit connection of phase and appropriate terminology echoes the coupling of phase and level of abstraction.Clearly, working at the appropriate level of abstraction is more than using the appropriate terminology-it is about using the appropriate level of detail.Nevertheless, PAPE 2 's underlying perspective of coupling, of parallelizing two scales, supports Armoni's recommendation for using terminology as a scaffolding for promoting abstraction, and specifically the ability to "decide, in every phase of the problemsolving process, at which level of abstraction it is appropriate to work" [4, p. 273].Note that as was the case for other representations of the problem-solving process, including the PGK hierarchy, the diagonal does not imply a one-direction top-down process.The skill of oscillating between levels of abstraction, going up and down as necessary, is inherent in the process.For example, after devising a solution, as expressed by the pair (3,3), and implementing it (the pair (2, 2)), the execution (expressed by the pair (1, 1) may result in a wrong output, indicating a bug.Using a debugger (the pair (1, 1)), the solver may find one or more erroneous statements in the program (the pair (2, 2)), and then ascend to the Algorithm level (the pair (3,3)) to mend the solution.
The lower part -using lower levels of algorithmic abstraction

The lower part of Figure 1 represents cases like those revealed in Studies 1 and 2, where a phase in the problem-solving solution is performed at an abstraction level that is lower than the appropriate one.Since one of the abilities of good algorithmic abstraction is to decide, in every phase of the problem-solving process, at which level of abstraction it is appropriate to work, pairs from the lower part indicate lower abstraction performance.

To show the high expressiveness of PAPE 2 , we will now exemplify all the pairs in the lower part.For the problem phase we will show two examples for each pair, from the learner's angle, who at this phase needs to understand a given problem, and the teacher's angle, who at this phase needs to compose an appropriate problem to pose to the students.

(4, 3) -The problem phase at the algorithm abstraction level.The problem phase should not involve solutions or any part of them.Thinking about solutions at this point may divert attention and prevent one from focusing on the problem.This may occur when a teacher presents a problem whose description involves directions towards a solution.For example, when presenting the problem "Use binary search to determine whether a student named name appears in the alphabetical list L of all the students in faculty F".This description blurs the difference between the two abstraction levels and is not compatible with Armoni's framework for teaching algorithmic abstraction [4].If one wants to add a hint or directions for the students, it is better to separate them from the problem's description and add them after it.

Another example is of a situation in which a solver who takes an operational view upon trying to understand a given problem [22].Namely, the solver interprets the problem by a 'how' perspective, rather than a 'what' perspective.Consider the problem, "Given a list Loans of books loaned from the library last month, sorted by the loan date, find the latest loan of the book book".A solver may be satisfied by self-explaining the problem as follows: "It means that if we look at all the loans of book in Loans, we should provide the last one".However, such a description is operational and may lead one to think that all the loans of the required book should be traversed in order to find the last one.In contrast, the declarative observation that the last loan of book is the one after which there is no other loan of book can lead the solver to traverse the list in reverse order, starting from the last loan until book is found for the first time.

(4, 2) -The problem phase at the program abstraction level.This pair was demonstrated in Section 3.2 for Study 2, by a problem whose description included programming-related terms.Similarly, a solver may exhibit a corresponding behavior when trying to understand a given problem by means of concrete programming terms.For example, by self-explaining the library loans task as follows: "So, I need to find i, where in the array Loans the book book is in Loans[i], and for every greater number j book is not in Loans[j]".

(4, 1) -The problem phase at the execution abstraction level.A problem description may correspond to this pair if it involves hints or directions that belong to the execution phase, for example, "integrate in the program print instructions to check different breakpoints".Like the pair (4, 3), it is better to separate such directions from the problem description.Another example is of a solver who tries to understand a given problem by examining its required output for one specific input.
(3, 2) -The algorithm phase at the program abstraction level.This pair was demonstrated in Section 3.1 for Study 1 by an algorithm that included programming-related terms.

(3, 1) -The algorithm phase at the execution abstraction level.Consider a teaching episode in which a teacher starts devising a solution for a given problem by decomposing it into sub-tasks.Instead of describing each of the sub-tasks verbally, the teacher explains them using screenshots of the Scratch environment, that depict the result of the sub-tasks in specific cases.

(2, 1) -The algorithm phase at the execution abstraction level.Consider a solution process in Scratch in which the solver executes instructions (by clicking the corresponding blocks) during the programming phase.Although this may serve as a certain type of scaffolding, it blurs the difference between the program as a general entity that should respond to every legitimate input (namely, any external legitimate event) and an execution in which the program runs with a specific sequence of legitimate external events.
The upper part -using higher levels of algorithmic abstraction

During the process of algorithmic problem solving, working at levels of abstraction that are higher than those corresponding to the solution phase may prove beneficial.Again, we will exemplify each of the six pairs in the upper part by a situation from a problemsolving context that is expressed by this pair.

(3, 4) -The algorithm phase at the problem abstraction level.As described in Section 2.2, the algorithm phase may involve alternating transitions between what and how.When a sub-task is solved, one is dealing with how it is done, and this is performed at the algorithm abstraction level.However, in a higher-level situation, a student can view a sub-task as a problem, using what it does as part of the solution.Doing that requires the ability to work with algorithmic black boxes.Namely, perceiving the sub-task as an input-output relation, and ignoring its solution idea or its implementation details.This demonstrates a high algorithmic abstraction ability, which students often fail to achieve [6].

(2, 4) -The program phase at the problem abstraction level.Invoking a user-defined subroutine (e.g., a function in functional programming, a procedure or a function in procedural programming, or a method in object-oriented programming), involves using black-box components when programming, counting only on what is done without knowing how it is done.Somewhat similarly, when utilizing library functions a programmer needs only to consider their "what" information and ignore their inner details.Research shows that despite the similarity between invoking user-defined subroutines and using library functions, in the sense of employing black boxes, novices may have difficulties with user-defined procedural encapsulation, especially if they use a user-defined procedure programmed by someone else [29].

(1, 4) -The execution phase at the problem abstraction level.This pair can express a situation of a student performing black-box testing.Such tests refer only to the description of the problem and ignore the algorithmic idea of the solution or the implementation details.

(2, 3) -The program phase at the algorithm abstraction level.For example, when programming in Scratch, the process of joining blocks to create scripts may shed light on the level of abstraction used by the programmer.Students that work at the Algorithm level tend to create their scripts by organizing their blocks in meaningful chunks rather than sequentially adding blocks or even using bricolage [45].Such observed situations are expressed by this pair.

(1, 3) -The execution phase at the algorithm abstraction level.Like the pair (1,4), this pair can be exemplified by black-box testing; however, at the Algorithm level, black-box testing is used for testing units or blocks of code with a unified algorithmic role.

(1, 2) -The execution phase at the program abstraction level.Unlike the previous pair, the program abstraction level can be exhibited in the execution phase by a student employing white-box testing, namely, considering the flow structure of the program (e.g., if statements, loops).
DISCUSSION AND CONCLUSIONS

We presented PAPE 2 , a generalized model for performing algorithmic abstraction.This model is composed of couplings of phases in the algorithmic problem-solving process and levels of algorithmic abstraction, obtained by Cartesian-squaring the four PGK levels.The creation of this model was based on generalizing findings obtained in two empirical studies, which exhibited two types of situations in which a certain phase at the algorithmic problem-solving process was performed at a low level of abstraction.Both studies used qualitative content analysis (discourse analysis and document analysis, respectively).This included a deductive content analysis, which started with the basic PGK hierarchy, and was then followed by an inductive content analysis, which exposed grounded types of observed behaviors relevant to algorithmic problem solving.Considering these specific grounded types of behaviors together suggested that in general, ordered pairs of solution process phases and abstraction levels express additional behaviors that may take place in algorithmic problem solving, thus leading to a grounded theory concerning the possible relationships between the phases of the algorithmic problem-solving process and levels of algorithmic abstraction.Note that we use grounded theory in a generalized form, since here, the theory (namely, the connections specified by PAPE 2 ) emerged from two studies.However, the data in both studies encapsulated algorithmic problem-solving processes that were analyzed using a joint perspective (since both analyses started in a deductive phase that used the same category system).Hence, the two studies can be viewed as two aspects of one exploration -that of algorithmic problem-solving processes -whose findings revealed a grounded model for such processes.

The potential contribution of PAPE 2 is significant, since it is a very generic, flexible model, which can be used to assess abstraction as reflected in various CS tasks, rather than being limited to specific diagnostic problems.It can be used in all aspects of teaching and learning algorithmic abstraction, rather than just for assessing students' learning outcomes, and when referring to abstraction in its full sense throughout the process of algorithmic problem solving, rather than just programming.Hence, it can serve to assess the quality of algorithmic problem solving in different educational contexts and regarding different educational aspects, including elaborate curricula, teaching materials, teachers' knowledge, and students' performance.In particular, it can be used by researchers and educators to assess the effectiveness of educational interventions aimed at developing learners' abstraction skills.When used for formative assessment, it can help to identify more accurately areas where students are struggling and it can provide targeted instruction to support growth in algorithmic abstraction skills.Since the onedirectional hierarchy underlying this model is now also connected to certain formal national curricula that emphasize levels of abstraction in the context of problem solving [e.g., 32], PAPE 2 has a direct large-scale contribution.

Moreover, the model is general also because it easily accommodates different perspectives of algorithmic abstraction that are found in the CSE research literature, beyond that of the PGK hierarchy or LOA.For example, Ginat's perspective on declarative vs. operational observations [21] (as was demonstrated in Section 4.3 regarding the couple (4, 3)), black-boxing [6] (as demonstrated in Section 4.4.regarding the couples (3,4), (2,4), and (1, 4), in the sense of algorithmic reduction, programming with subroutines, and testing, respectively), and Armoni's framework for teaching algorithmic abstraction (as discussed in Section 4.2).Therefore, it also has the potential to serve as a rich unifying model for CSE researchers when discussing different aspects of algorithmic abstraction.

Furthermore, PAPE 2 resonates with the philosophical views of leading CS pioneers such as Dijkstra regarding CS abstraction, easily depicting different forms of oscillation between levels of abstraction.In section 4.2 we mentioned how the oscillating nature of the solution process can be expressed using the diagonal.In Section 4.4 we referred to oscillation between 'what' and 'how' in the algorithm phase.Unlike the oscillation along the diagonal, in which both parts of the pair change together, the oscillation in the algorithm phase is reflected in the pairs' second element, whereas the first is stable at 3. Namely, it involves the diagonal (the pair (3,3)) and the upper part (the pair (3,4)).Oscillation between 'what' and 'how' in the programming phase, namely, between defining subroutines and invoking them, is depicted similarly, moving back and forth between the pairs (2, 2) and (2,4).

Like any assessment model, PAPE 2 can also be used to guide teaching.The diagonal of the model, which depicts an axis along which the solution process should oscillate, represents recommended teaching guidelines.The less desired behaviors, expressed in the lower part of the model, represent coupling that should be avoided by the teachers when demonstrating algorithmic abstraction (e.g., using programming terms when devising an algorithmic solution).Nevertheless, they should be utilized as teaching opportunities when performed by students.The upper part expresses situations that employ algorithmic abstraction even further.As exemplified in Section 4.4, it represents more complicated behaviors than those included in the diagonal.In particular, as was just mentioned, the combination of the upper part and the diagonal captures oscillations between 'what' and 'how', that is, the skill of opening and closing black boxes, when appropriate.In line with this, integrating the upper-part problem-solving behaviors in teaching may foster the development of algorithmic abstraction skills and may even promote the acquisition of advanced skills (such as using black boxes when devising solutions and for testing them).The effect of such a teaching approach has yet to be studied.This is a theoretical work, anchored in the research literature and grounded in research findings, which opens several research directions.Future research efforts can demonstrate the applicability of PAPE 2 for assessment in different contexts and for different purposes.Additional research is needed to study the effectiveness of educational strategies that employ PAPE 2 to guide the teaching of algorithmic abstraction.Previous research [45] that studied the applicability of Armoni's framework [4] for teaching algorithmic abstraction in middle school showed its effectiveness in general and also found that following a short training the teachers could use it satisfactorily, except for the principle of linguistic aid, which they tended not to follow.Considering the apparent association between this principle and PAPE 2 , discussed in Section 4.2, an interesting potential research direction would be to study a similar teaching strategy that is based on PAPE 2 , examine the extent to which teachers adopt the principle of linguistic aid when employing this strategy, and compare the effectiveness of the PAPE 2 -based strategy and the one suggested by Armoni.
